topic: How chassis dynos and correction standards read, so real dyno sheets can be normalised to the simulation's target: roller inertia dyno (Dynojet-type) wheel power, SAE J1349 corrected.

mostReliable: Correction formulas: EEC 80/1269 as amended (legal text read): αa = (99/ps)^1.2 · (T/298)^0.6, 25 °C / 99 kPa dry, valid only 0.93-1.07 and 15-35 °C. Dynojet's 'SAE' (own manual): CF = 1.18 · (99/pd) · sqrt(T/298) − 0.18 (J1349 JUN90, 85 % mechanical efficiency). SuperFlow's default 'SAE' has no friction term; MAHA's 'SAE' uses the ISO-type exponents. DIN 70020 (MAHA): (1013/p) · sqrt(T/293), total pressure.
STD (J607) vs SAE (J1349): Ford Racing says about 4 %. Recomputed from the formulas: 1.040 at 25 °C / 99 kPa, 1.034 at 45 °C, about 1.05 in cold air.

Best-controlled same-car test (Road & Track 2026, Dark Horse 6MT, 5th = 1:1, SAE, same week): vs Dynojet 248X 425.7 whp → Dynapack 1.012, SuperFlow 0.988, Mustang AWD 1.092. Dynojet whp was 0.851 of Ford's 500 hp rating.

DSPORT 2016 (same Supra and EVO IX on five dynos; conditions not stated): vs Dynojet 424xLC2 → Rototest 0.91-0.93, Dynapack 0.99-1.01 on the RWD car but 0.90-0.95 on the AWD car, Mustang 0.84-0.88 RWD but 1.00-1.02 AWD, SuperFlow 0.84-0.91.

Losses: component literature gives manual gearbox 92-97 % and hypoid axle 90-95 % at full load, with torque-dependent and torque-independent parts. On a MAHA twin-roller dyno a 2.0 RWD manual in 4th showed wheel/engine 0.85-0.87 at low and mid rpm, falling to 0.83 at 5000 and 0.74 at 6000 rpm because the loss grows with speed.
Dyno makers themselves model loss as speed-dependent (coast-down) plus a small torque-proportional share: SuperFlow K = 0.07-0.09 for manuals, up to 0.30 for automatics.

Sweep effects (Mustang manual): fast accelerating sweeps read lowest, longer sweeps read higher; inertia effect scales with overall ratio squared (top gear about 3 % of 1st). Pulls are made in the 1:1 gear (Ford, Dynojet, MAHA). Leaving out wheel inertia can cut an acceleration-test reading by up to 10 % (SuperFlow).
biggestDoubts: There is no single Mustang-to-Dynojet factor: measured ratios run from 0.84 to 1.09 depending on the car (RWD vs AWD), the software mode and the shop. The popular '10-15 % lower' only held for the RWD Supra.

Dyno Dynamics and Mainline ratios (about 15 % and 15-18 % below Dynojet) come only from experienced tuners on forums. On Dyno Dynamics even the wheel figure moves by about 15 % between shootout classes, so a DD sheet without its class is hard to use.
Whether a sheet is SAE, STD or uncorrected is often not printed. Dynojet's factory default and any date it changed from STD to SAE were not found.
The project default of 45 °C ambient is outside the 15-35 °C range that SAE J1349 (AUG2004) and EEC 80/1269 intend their corrections for; corrected numbers from very hot days are extrapolations.
Density corrections can over-correct modern boost-controlled turbo engines (auto motor und sport, MAHA/Porsche case). This matters for S15, JZA80 and FD3S sheets.

Fixed-vs-proportional loss on a Dynojet has no clean controlled test; the best same-car evidence is one forum anecdote (C5 Corvette, ~80 hp constant from 440 to 615 hp). The MAHA data comes from a twin-roller dyno, which has more tyre loss than a single Dynojet drum.
DSPORT did not state correction, gear or test dates; R&T is only one car.

dynoTypes.ratio: Supra (RWD): 0.883 at low boost, 0.840 at high boost (peak to peak). EVO IX (AWD): 1.023 at low boost, 0.995 at high boost. So the Mustang read 12-16 % lower on the RWD car but about the same or slightly higher on the AWD car.

corrections.standard: SAE J1349 (JUN1990 revision) as implemented by Dynojet WinPEP ('SAE' on Dynojet sheets)
corrections.reference: 25 °C (77 °F), 99 kPa dry air pressure (Dynojet prints 29.22 inHg and 537 °R; 99 kPa = 29.235 inHg), 0 % humidity
corrections.formula: CF = 1.18 × (29.22 / Bdo) × sqrt((To + 460) / 537) − 0.18, with To = intake air temperature in °F and Bdo = dry ambient absolute pressure in inHg. Same thing in SI: CF = 1.18 × (99 / pd[kPa]) × sqrt((T[°C] + 273) / 298) − 0.18.
corrections.notes: The 1.18 / −0.18 form is the J1349 friction assumption: Dynojet says it 'assumes a mechanical efficiency of 85%'. Dynojet applies it to the wheel power it measures. Dynojet's printed 29.22 inHg looks like a rounding slip for 29.23-29.235 inHg (99 kPa); other Dynojet and SuperFlow material uses 29.23/29.235. Ford quotes the J1349 conditions as '77 deg F inlet air, 29.31 inHg barometric pressure', which does not match 99 kPa dry exactly (maybe a total-pressure figure; not explained).

sources.quote: p. 9-5: "Dynojet's WinPEP (Performance Evaluation Program for Windows 95) software uses the SAE's latest correction formula (June 1990). This formula assumes a mechanical efficiency of 85% and is much more accurate than earlier formulas at extreme conditions. The formula used is: CF= 1.18 x (29.22/Bdo) x √(To+460 / 537) - 0.18 Where: To = Intake air temperature in degrees F Bdo = Dry ambient absolute barometric pressure" (square-root sign confirmed on the rendered page)

corrections.notes: Numerically almost the same as the JUN90 form (difference under 0.05 % in normal conditions; see the derived entry below). The 2004 revision prefers measured friction power and keeps 85 % mechanical efficiency only as a fallback. The standard itself (SAE, paid) was not read; this comes from a careful secondary page. sources.quote: "In August 2004 the SAE released J1349 Revised AUG2004 which specifies that the preferred method of determining the friction power used by the motor accessories is actual measurement, and that the assumption of 85% mechanical efficiency (as formerly used in SAE J1349 Revision JUN90) should only be used when actual friction data are not available." Equation image reads: cf = 1.176 · [(990/Pd) · ((Tc + 273)/298)^0.5] − 0.176. "Section 5.1 of the SAE J1349 AUG2004 revision also makes it clear that this correction factor is not intended to provide accurate corrections over an extremely wide range, but rather that the intended range of air temperatures is 15 to 35 deg C, and the intended range of dry air pressures is 900 to 1050 mb."

corrections.standard: 'SAE J1349' as SuperFlow WinDyn implements it by default (AutoDyn 30 config)
corrections.formula: SAECor = ((459.7 + AirInT[°F]) / 536.7)^0.5 × (29.23 / (Baro_P − Vap_P)) — a plain density ratio with NO 1.18 / −0.18 friction term
corrections.notes: So an 'SAE' number is not the same on every dyno brand. Near 25 °C / 99 kPa the two forms agree; at 45 °C / 99 kPa the SuperFlow form is about 0.6 % lower than the Dynojet form (derived). SuperFlow also leaves coast-down losses uncorrected when it estimates engine power.

This factor estimates what the measured torque and power would be at 77° Fahrenheit [25°C] and 29.23 inches of mercury [99 kPa] air pressure." ... "NOTE: The correction factors listed below are the default formulas provided by SuperFlow. WinDyn is capable of generating performance data corrected to any standard." ... corrections.standard: SAE J607 ('STD' or 'STP' on many dyno sheets)
corrections.formula: STPCor = ((459.7 + T[°F]) / 519.7)^0.5 × 29.92 / (Baro_P − Vap_P) (SuperFlow's default channel). No friction term.
corrections.notes: Size of gap: Ford Racing says J1349 is 'typically about 4% lower' than J607; Fuel Moto says STD is 2-4 % higher; Dynojet only says STD 'often results in a higher displayed horsepower number'. The derived entry below gives 1.040 at the J1349 reference point and 1.034 at 45 °C. One unverified search snippet (forum page blocked) described a WinPEP 'standard corrected' mode using 29.92 inHg and 68 °F; this conflicts with the 60 °F used by SuperFlow, Fuel Moto and J607 and could not be checked. Fuel Moto says STD 'was canceled in 1988' (secondary source, not verified). SuperFlow's printed channel 102 has misplaced brackets ('/519.7^0.5*(29.92/Baro_P-Vap_P)'); the formula given here is the evident intended form, matching its own description (60 °F, 29.92 inHg). Fuel Moto's SAE reference '29.60 inHg, 36 % humidity' at 77 °F works out to about 99.1 kPa dry, so it is consistent with 99 kPa dry (researcher's check).

drivetrainLoss.finding: A dyno maker models chassis-dyno loss as a speed-dependent part (measured on coast-down) PLUS a small torque-proportional part.
drivetrainLoss.numbers: SuperFlow AutoDyn: loss = C_DLos + (WhlPwr − C_DLos) × K_Fact, with K_Fact 0.07-0.09 for manuals (default 0.07) and up to 0.30 for automatics. Coast-down 'measures all of the speed dependent losses, but only a fraction of the torque dependent losses'.

sources.title: SuperFlow, AutoDyn-30-2WD Chassis Dyno Configuration File Description, Pub. No. 200507 Rev. 2, June 2020
sources.quote: "77 - K_Fact 0.0700 Channel 77 is an Engine Power channel for entering the K_Factor for drivetrain losses. This value specifies what percentage of the total drivetrain losses on a vehicle are Torque Dependent vs. Speed Dependent. ... During a coast down, the dyno measures all of the speed dependent losses, but only a fraction of the torque dependent losses. The torque that is going through the vehicle drivetrain during coast down is much less than it was during the acceleration run. ... Typical values for manual transmission vehicles are 0.07 - 0.09. Automatic equipped vehicles may require values as high as 0.30. The default value is 0.07." ... "66 - EsDTLs hp return(C_DLos+(WhlPwr-C_DLos)*K_Fact);"

drivetrainLoss.strength: medium (dyno maker's model, not a measurement)

drivetrainLoss.finding: Mustang's software also splits losses: a speed-dependent vehicle-loss curve (A + B·v + C·v², from a coast-down 'Characterize Vehicle Losses' test) plus a drivetrain efficiency percentage for 'engine' figures. It publishes typical component efficiencies.
drivetrainLoss.numbers: Typical (2017): manual transmission 90-97 %, automatic 90-95 %, CVT 87-93 %, hypoid differential 90-95 %, spiral bevel 95-99 %, straight bevel 93-97 %; RWD overall = transmission × differential. Manual × hypoid gives 81-92 % overall (researcher's multiplication).

sources.title: Mustang Dynamometer, POWER DYNE PC Operator Manual (v2017-05-22)
sources.quote: p. 43: "Drivetrain Efficiency (%) The overall drivetrain efficiency, from crankshaft to tires. Typical current (2017) values for some drivetrain components are given below: Item Typical efficiency range Manual transmission 90% - 97% Automatic transmission 90% - 95% CVT transmission 87% - 93% Hypoid differential 90% - 95% Spiral bevel differential 95% - 99% Straight bevel differential 93% - 97% For rear-wheel drive vehicles, you must multiply the transmission and differential values to get overall efficiency." p. 42: "Vehicle Losses Curve A, B, C The coefficients for a force(speed) curve representing the extra losses incurred, above the dynamometer's parasitic losses, from having the vehicle on the dynamometer. These values are normally obtained using the “Characterize Vehicle Losses” function" ... "Force = (A) + (B*Speed) + (C*Speed^2)"

drivetrainLoss.finding: Gearbox losses split into a torque-dependent part (gear mesh, loaded bearings) and a torque-independent part (seals, churning, rotary unions). In the direct (1:1) gear no gear pair carries load. Typical full-load gearbox efficiencies are given.
drivetrainLoss.numbers: Full-load overall efficiency (Naunheimer, quoted by BMW co-authors): manual 92-97 %, automatic 90-95 %, mechanical CVT 87-93 %, hydrostatic CVT 80-86 %. In automatics, wet-clutch drag can exceed 50 % of the total loss.

sources.title: Schlegel (Schlegel Simulation), Hösl (BMW Group), Diel (UAS Landshut), 'Detailed Loss Modelling of Vehicle Gearboxes', 7th Modelica Conference 2009, DOI 10.3384/ecp09430059
sources.quote: "Naunheimer [3] gives a rough survey of typical overall efficiencies of vehicle gearboxes under full load: Manual gearbox 92 - 97 %, Automatic gearbox 90 – 95 %, Mechanical CVT 87 – 93 %, Hydrostatic CVT 80 – 86 %" ... "Losses of gears and bearings may be split up into a part depending on the transmitted torque and a torque independent part. ... Torque independent losses arise even if no torque is transmitted but the shafts rotate." ... "the losses of wet multi-disc clutches in automatic gearboxes can account for even more than 50 % of the total power loss." ... "In the 7 th gear, which is engaged by direct coupling of input and output shaft ... no gears are loaded in this case."

sweepEffects.finding: Faster accelerating sweeps read lower; steady-state reads more; decelerating sweeps read highest, because the engine and driveline absorb power to accelerate their own inertia.

sweepEffects.finding: Longer sweep time (lower acceleration rate) gives higher readings; Mustang recommends the longest sweep the car tolerates.

sources.title: Mustang Dynamometer, POWER DYNE PC Operator Manual (v2017-05-22)
sources.quote: p. 136: "A longer sweep time should generate higher power and torque readings, since a lower acceleration rate means that less power is absorbed by the vehicle's drive train." p. 134: "Mustang Dynamometer recommends that you use the longest running time that the vehicle can comfortably tolerate"

sweepEffects.finding: Driveline inertia seen by the dyno scales with overall gear ratio squared, so a low gear exaggerates inertia effects; top gear shows only a few percent of the first-gear effect.
sweepEffects.numbers: Gear ratios span about 6:1, so about 36:1 in inertia effect; top gear about 3 % of first gear.

sources.title: Mustang Dynamometer, POWER DYNE PC Operator Manual (v2017-05-22)
sources.quote: p. 43: "This value will be large in 1st gear, and much smaller in top gear, as inertial effects are proportional to the overall gear ratio squared. Transmission gear ratios vary over about a 6:1 range, so squared that is 36:1, so the inertial effect in top gear may only be about 3% of the effect in 1st gear."

sweepEffects.finding: Pulls are made in the 1:1 gear because efficiency drops away from 1:1 and because acceleration-related effects (engine, gearbox and wheel inertia, tyres) change with gear and axle ratio.

sources.title: Ford Racing Performance Parts, 'Dynamometer Testing and Ford Racing Calibrations' (undated PDF)
sources.quote: "Most chassis dyno tests are performed using the “roll-on” method ... Because of this constant acceleration, engine and transmission inertia, drive wheel inertia, tire characteristics, gear ratio and axle ratio can all affect the final measured horsepower. Generally a heavier wheel will take more torque to accelerate at the same rate as a lighter wheel, so heavier wheels will tend to reduce the measured wheel horsepower. Gear ratio comes into play because as the gear ratio strays from a 1:1, the efficiency drops and therefore the measured horsepower at the wheels also drops. This is why most dyno runs are run in the 1:1 gear (i.e., 4th gear in a 5-speed overdrive transmission) whenever possible."
